en: Dīgha Nikāya 6 Mahālisutta 1. The Account of the Brahmin Messenger [The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time, a certain brahmin messenger from the Licchavis had arrived at Sāvatthī on some business. He went to the Blessed One, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, the Licchavis of Vesālī are in good health and well-being. They ask after Master Gotama’s health and well-being: ‘Is Master Gotama in good health? Is he free from illness and discomfort? “I am in good health, friend,” the Blessed One replied. “And the Licchavis of Vesālī are also in good health. Then the brahmin messenger said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, the Licchavis of Vesālī are saying this: ‘We have heard that the ascetic Gotama says, “Only my teaching is true; other teachings are false; only my discipline is true; other disciplines are false. Master Gotama, do the Licchavis speak truthfully, or do they speak falsely? “Friend, the Licchavis do not speak truthfully when they say that; they speak falsely. For it is not the case that I say, ‘Only my teaching is true; other teachings are false; only my discipline is true; other disciplines are false. “But, Master Gotama, how is it that you do not say such a thing? “Friend, I do not say, ‘Only my teaching is true; other teachings are false; only my discipline is true; other disciplines are false. Rather, friend, I say this: ‘Whether it be my own teaching or the teaching of another, if it is conducive to the good, conducive to the wholesome, conducive to the beneficial, conducive to happiness, and leads to the ultimate goal of Nibbāna—that is true; the rest is false. Whether it be my own discipline or the discipline of another, if it is conducive to the good, conducive to the wholesome, conducive to the beneficial, conducive to happiness, and leads to the ultimate goal of Nibbāna—that is true; the rest is false. When this was said, the brahmin messenger said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! It is as if someone were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Just so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. [The Blessed One then taught him the Dhamma, and the brahmin messenger, having heard the Dhamma, attained the fruit of stream-entry. [End of the first section: The Account of the Brahmin Messenger]
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, many brahmin messengers from Kosala and many brahmin messengers from Magadha were staying at Vesālī on some business or other.
The Brahmin messengers from Kosala and the Brahmin messengers from Magadha heard:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
A fine report concerning the venerable Gotama has spread abroad thus:"

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear vision and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having personally realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, by means of direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure.
"It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then those brahmin messengers from Kosala and those brahmin messengers from Magadha approached the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest.
Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgita was the Blessed One’s attendant.
Then those brahmin messengers from Kosala and those brahmin messengers from Magadha approached the Venerable Nāgita. Having approached, they said this to the Venerable Nāgita:
"Where, Master Nāgita, does that Blessed One Gotama dwell at present?
For we are desirous of seeing that Blessed One Gotama."
“It is not the right time, friends, to see the Blessed One; the Blessed One is in seclusion.
Then those brahmin messengers from Kosala and those brahmin messengers from Magadha sat down right there to one side, saying:
“We shall go only after we have seen that venerable Gotama.”
2. The Story of Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi.
Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi, together with a great assembly of Licchavis, approached the Venerable Nāgita at the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Nāgita and sat down to one side.
He stood to one side. Standing there, Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi said this to the Venerable Nāgita:
"Where, venerable Nāgita, does the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell at present?
For we wish to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
“Mahāli, it is not the right time to see the Blessed One; the Blessed One is in seclusion.
Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi sat down right there to one side, thinking:
“I will go to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, once I have seen him myself.”
Then the novice Sīha approached the Venerable Nāgita;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Nāgita and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the novice Sīha said this to the Venerable Nāgita:
"Venerable Kassapa, these many Brahmin messengers from Kosala and Brahmin messengers from Magadha..."
They have come here to see the Blessed One; Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi too has come here with a great assembly of Licchavis to see the Blessed One.
It would be well, venerable Kassapa, if this multitude were to obtain a sight of the Blessed One.”
“In that case, Sīha, you yourself inform the Blessed One.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the novice Sīha replied to the Venerable Nāgita.
He then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side...
Standing there, the novice Sīha said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, these many brahmin messengers from Kosala and brahmin messengers from Magadha have arrived here to see the Blessed One;
and Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi has also arrived here together with a great assembly of Licchavis."
“...to see the Blessed One.
It would be well, Bhante, if this multitude might obtain the opportunity to see the Blessed One.
“In that case, Sīha, prepare a seat in the shade of the monastery,” [the Blessed One said].
“Yes, Bhante,” the novice Sīha replied to the Blessed One and prepared a seat in the shade of the dwelling.
Then the Blessed One emerged from the dwelling and sat down on the seat prepared in the shade of the dwelling.
Then those brahmin messengers from Kosala and those brahmin messengers from Magadha approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, they sat down to one side.
Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi also approached the Blessed One together with a large assembly of Licchavis;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. While sitting there, Oṭṭhaddha—
The Licchavis said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, in former days, long ago, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached me; having approached, he said this to me:
‘Mahāli, it has not been long since I have been living in dependence upon the Blessed One—only three years. Divine...’”
“I see forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust, yet I do not hear divine sounds that are lovely,
connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. “Venerable sir,
were those divine sounds that Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son did not hear— those which are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust— actually present, or were they not?”

2.1. Concentration Developed One-Sidedly “Mahāli, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son did not hear only those divine sounds that were present—those that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion; he did not hear those that were absent.

“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son did not hear only those divine sounds that were present—those that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion—and did not hear those that were absent?”
“Here, Mahāli, a bhikkhu possesses concentration developed in one direction:

for seeing celestial forms that are lovely, desirable, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing; yet he does not possess concentration for hearing celestial sounds that are lovely, desirable, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing.
Thus, in the eastern direction, he has cultivated one-sided concentration for the purpose of seeing divine forms—
forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and alluring— but not for the purpose of hearing divine sounds— sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and alluring.

He sees divine forms in the eastern direction— forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and alluring— but he does not hear divine sounds— sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and alluring.
For what reason? Because it is so, Mahāli,
that for a bhikkhu whose concentration is developed one-pointedly in the eastern direction for the purpose of seeing celestial forms—
forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion— there is yet no such [power] regarding celestial sounds.
for the sake of hearing things that are dear, connected with sensual pleasures, and alluring.
Furthermore, Mahāli, for a bhikkhu from the southern direction …pe… from the western direction … [and so on].
In the northern direction... above, below, and across, there is concentration developed in one way for the seeing of divine forms— forms that are lovely,
connected with sensual desire, and enticing— but not for the hearing of divine sounds— sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and enticing.
Thus, when concentration is developed in one direction— upward, downward, and across—
it leads to the seeing of divine forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and alluring, but not to the hearing of divine sounds that are lovely,

connected with sensual desire, and alluring. Upward, downward, and across, he sees divine forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and alluring, but he does not hear divine sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and alluring.
And why is that? Because, Mahāli,
it is so for a bhikkhu when his concentration is developed in one way— upward, downward, and across—
for the purpose of seeing divine forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion, but not for hearing divine sounds.
For the hearing of sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of passion. Here, Mahāli, a bhikkhu possesses concentration developed in one direction for the hearing of divine sounds that are lovely,
connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion, but not yet for the seeing of divine forms.
[This refers to] forms that are dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
He possesses a concentration developed in one direction for the hearing of divine sounds that are dear,
connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust, but not for the seeing of divine forms that are dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
In the eastern direction, he hears divine sounds—dear, connected with sensual desire, and enticing—but he does not see divine forms—dear, connected with sensual desire, and enticing.
For what reason?
Because, Mahāli, it is when a bhikkhu has cultivated one-pointed concentration in the eastern direction that such divine [sounds] [occur].

for the hearing of sounds that are dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust, but not for the seeing of divine forms that are dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
Furthermore, Mahāli, for a bhikkhu from the southern direction... [and so on].
In the western direction … in the northern direction … above,
below, across, there is concentration developed in one way for the hearing of heavenly sounds that are pleasant.

He does not possess concentration cultivated in one direction for the purpose of seeing divine forms— forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion— but he possesses concentration cultivated in one direction for the purpose of hearing divine sounds—

sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion. He does not possess concentration cultivated in one direction for the purpose of seeing divine forms— forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion— but he possesses concentration cultivated in one direction for the purpose of hearing divine sounds— sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion— above, below, and across.
Above, below, and across, he hears divine sounds—pleasant, connected with sensual desire, and enticing—but he does not see divine forms—pleasant, connected with sensual desire, and enticing.
For what reason?
Because it is so, Mahāli, that for a bhikkhu whose concentration is developed one-pointedly above, below, and across, there are [only] divine [sounds].
for the hearing of sounds that are dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust, but not for the seeing of divine forms that are dear,
connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Here, Mahāli,
a bhikkhu possesses a concentration cultivated in both ways regarding the eastern direction, and [concerning] divine forms...

For the seeing of forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion; and for the hearing of divine sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion.
He, through the concentration developed in both ways, [attains] the seeing of divine forms that are lovely... in the eastern direction.
For the sake of hearing divine sounds that are connected with sensual pleasure, lovely, and enticing;

and in the eastern direction he sees divine forms that are lovely, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing, and he hears divine sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing.
For what reason is that?
In this way, Mahāli, it comes about for a bhikkhu that when his concentration is developed in both ways regarding the eastern direction,
he possesses the divine sight of beautiful forms associated with sensual desire and provocative of lust,
and the divine hearing of beautiful sounds associated with sensual desire and provocative of lust.
Furthermore, Mahāli, for a bhikkhu in the southern direction … in the western direction … in the northern direction … [the same applies].
There is concentration developed in both ways—upward, downward, and across—for the seeing of celestial forms that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion;
and for the hearing of celestial sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of passion.
When he has concentration developed in both ways—upward, downward, and across—for the seeing of celestial forms that are lovely... [he sees them].
For the sake of hearing divine sounds that are connected with sensual desire, pleasing, and alluring;

and he sees divine forms, above, below, and across, that are pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and alluring; and he hears divine sounds, above, below, and across, that are pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and alluring.
For what reason is that?
For it is thus, Mahāli, that for a bhikkhu whose concentration is developed in both ways—
upward, downward, and across— there comes about the seeing of celestial forms, lovely, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of lust; and the hearing of celestial sounds, lovely, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

“This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the reason why Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, heard only those divine sounds that exist—sounds that are lovely, connected with sensual pleasure, and enticing—and not those that do not exist.
“Venerable sir, surely it is for the sake of realizing these developments of concentration that monks lead the holy life under the Blessed One?
“Mahāli, it is not for the sake of realizing these developments of concentration that monks lead the holy life under me.”
“Mahāli, there are indeed other teachings that are higher and more sublime than these, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.
“But what, Bhante, are those teachings that are higher and more sublime than these, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under the Blessed One?”
“Here, Mahāli, with the complete destruction of three fetters, a bhikkhu is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.
This, Mahāli, is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.

Furthermore, Mahāli, with the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, a bhikkhu is a once-returner; returning to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering.”
This, too, Mahāli, is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.
Furthermore, Mahāli, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, a bhikkhu becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.
This, too, Mahāli, is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.

"Furthermore, Mahāli, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
This too, Mahāli, is a Dhamma that is higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me.
These, Mahāli, are those Dhammas that are higher and more sublime, for the sake of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me."
“Venerable sir, is there a path, is there a way for the realization of these states? “There is indeed,
Mahāli, a path, there is a way for the realization of these states.”
“But what, venerable sir, is the path, what is the way for the realization of these states?
“This very Noble Eightfold Path. That is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
"This, Mahāli, is the path, this is the way for the realization of these states.
2.4. The Account of Two Wanderers:
Once, Mahāli, I was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park."
Then two wanderers, the ascetic Muṇḍiya and Jāliya the pupil of Dārupattika, approached me. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with me.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, those two wanderers said this to me:
“Now, friend Gotama, is that soul the same as this body, or is the soul one thing and the body another?
“In that case, friends, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, friend,” those two wanderers replied to me.
I said this:
“In this case, friends, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha...
[as before] ...In this way, friends, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue.”
He enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
Friend, is it appropriate for a bhikkhu who knows thus and sees thus to say: [“I am an arahant”]?
“Is it ‘the soul is the same as the body’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’?
“Friend, for a bhikkhu who knows thus and sees thus,
it is appropriate to say either ‘the soul is the same as the body’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another.’”
"But as for this, friend, I know it thus and I see it thus;
yet I do not say:
'the soul is the same as the body,' nor do I say: 'the soul is one thing and the body another'... [and so on].
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna.
"Friend, if a bhikkhu knows thus and sees thus, would it be appropriate for him to say,
'The soul is the same as the body,' or 'The soul is one thing and the body another'?
"Friend, if a bhikkhu knows thus and sees thus, it would indeed be appropriate for him to say that."
‘That which is the soul is the body,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another.
Yet, friends, it is thus that I know and thus that I see;
nevertheless, I do not say:
“‘The soul is the same as the body’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’ ...
[and so on] ... he directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision.
Friend, if a bhikkhu knows thus and sees thus, would it be appropriate for him to say:”
‘That which is the soul is the body,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’?
… [as before] … Friend, for a bhikkhu who knows thus and sees thus, it is appropriate to say: [that the soul is the body, or that the soul is one thing and the body another].”
‘That which is the soul is the body,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another.
Yet, friend, it is thus that I know and thus that I see;
nevertheless, I do not declare this:
‘That which is the soul is the body’ or ‘The soul is one thing and the body another.
…pe… He understands: “There is nothing further beyond this state of being.
Now, friends, regarding a bhikkhu who knows thus and sees thus, would it be appropriate for him to say: [“I do not know or see whether after death a Tathāgata exists”]?
"Is it the case that 'the soul is the same as the body' or that 'the soul is one thing and the body another'?
"Friend, for a bhikkhu who knows thus and sees thus,
it is not appropriate to say either 'the soul is the same as the body' or 'the soul is one thing and the body another'."
"But as for this, friend, I know it thus and see it thus;
yet I do not say:
'The soul is the same as the body,' nor do I say: 'The soul is one thing and the body another.'"
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The Licchavi Oṭṭhaddha, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Mahāli Sutta, the sixth, is concluded.
